paragraphs: This paper studies backdoor attacks against graph neural networks that classify nodes. A poisoned training graph can cause a model to assign an attacker-chosen category when a trigger is attached to a test node. The authors focus on attacks involving multiple target categories, where existing trigger generators struggle as the number of categories increases.

Their EUMC approach draws trigger subgraphs from the graph being attacked. This provides a source of existing graph structure with category-related information. The method organizes these subgraphs into a pool and uses changes in attachment probabilities as evidence about their target categories. A selection-and-attachment strategy then chooses suitable triggers with the aim of making the modifications less noticeable.

Experiments across real-world datasets, several graph neural networks, and defense strategies support the effectiveness of the approach. The central finding is that the attacked graph itself can supply useful category-aware triggers. This broadens the demonstrated backdoor threat beyond methods centered on a single target category.
neurips-2025-attack-by-yourself-effectiv.tldr: EUMC uses subgraphs from an attacked graph to create less noticeable backdoor triggers for multiple target categories.

paragraphs: Comparing two models often involves reducing the similarity of their internal representations to one number. That number summarizes agreement, but it does not explain which learned features the models share. This paper combines representation comparison with concept discovery to make those similarities more interpretable.

The method breaks alignment down into individual concepts, exposing both concepts shared across models and the organization of concepts within each model. The authors define concepts as nonlinear manifolds: structures that can follow curved shapes within a representation space. They hypothesize that this definition fits the geometry of learned features better than linear alternatives. A sanity check supports its advantage for the concept-based comparison they study.

The authors apply the analysis to four vision transformers. In this comparison, greater supervision tends to accompany less semantic organization in the learned representations. The finding is a tendency in the studied models, while the broader contribution is a way to explain what representational agreement consists of instead of reporting only its overall magnitude.
neurips-2025-beyond-scalars-concept-base.tldr: Concept-based alignment reveals which features vision transformers share and how those features are organized.

paragraphs: BraVE addresses offline reinforcement learning when an action consists of multiple discrete choices. The difficulty is that the number of complete actions grows exponentially with the number of component choices. Evaluating every combination becomes computationally impractical, even when each individual choice has relatively few possibilities.

A competing strategy is to factorize action values, but the abstract identifies a weakness in existing approaches: they fail to capture how component choices affect one another. BraVE, short for Branch Value Estimation, uses a tree-structured traversal of actions. This lets it evaluate a linear number of joint actions while retaining the dependency structure among their components.

The reported experiments involve environments with more than four million possible actions, where BraVE outperforms prior offline reinforcement learning methods by up to twentyfold. The stated result supports the usefulness of combining selective joint-action evaluation with dependency modeling. Its central contribution is a way to reduce the evaluation burden without discarding the interactions that make combinatorial decisions difficult.
neurips-2025-brave-offline-reinforcement.tldr: BraVE efficiently evaluates combinatorial actions through a tree structure while preserving dependencies between component choices.

paragraphs: Low-rank approximation reduces the complexity of neural network components for compression or fine-tuning. Context-aware versions weight approximation errors using input activations, so the approximation reflects how the network is used. The paper addresses a numerical problem in existing methods: explicitly forming and inverting Gram matrices can degrade approximation quality or produce matrices that are numerically singular.

COALA replaces those calculations with an inversion-free, regularized framework built from stable decompositions. The aim is to retain the benefits of activation-weighted approximation while avoiding unstable intermediate calculations. This makes numerical reliability a central part of the approximation procedure.

The framework handles calibration matrices too large for GPU memory, activation matrices close to singularity, and data shortages that prevent a unique approximation. For the insufficient-data case, the authors prove convergence to a desired approximation and provide explicit error bounds. These results matter because the usefulness of context-aware compression depends on obtaining a reliable approximation even when the available activation data are computationally or mathematically challenging.
neurips-2025-coala-numerically-stable-an.tldr: COALA makes context-aware low-rank approximation more numerically reliable through regularization and stable, inversion-free calculations.

paragraphs: CoC-VLA aims to connect two complementary sources of autonomous-driving knowledge. Real-world data support deployment, while simulation can represent rare or difficult situations such as accidents and unusual road-user behavior. The paper proposes a framework for transferring the handling of these long-tail situations from simulation into a model trained with real-world data.

The framework contains teacher and student vision-language models plus a discriminator. Teacher and student share a Chain-of-Causality architecture that incorporates temporal information through a text adapter and supports reasoning about complex driving situations. They are initially trained separately on simulated and real-world datasets. Adversarial training of the discriminator, together with a new backpropagation strategy, facilitates transfer to the student.

Experiments indicate that the method bridges the simulation-to-reality gap in the studied autonomous-driving setting. The contribution is an explicit mechanism for combining the strengths of both data sources within an end-to-end framework. Its reported success supports this transfer strategy as a promising research direction for difficult driving scenarios.
neurips-2025-coc-vla-delving-into-advers.tldr: CoC-VLA uses adversarial teacher–student transfer to bring simulated rare-scenario driving capabilities into a real-world student model.

paragraphs: Training a language model from rewards can be difficult when feedback arrives only after an entire answer. Sparse feedback increases variation in policy updates and makes estimating the value of intermediate reasoning states difficult. DAPO addresses this problem with an offline reinforcement learning algorithm that supplies feedback at individual reasoning steps.

The method uses a critic to provide dense signals for updating the actor, the model producing the reasoning. This gives the optimization process information at a finer level than assigning a uniform outcome-driven update direction to every step. DAPO also trains the actor and critic independently. The authors connect this separation to better value estimation and avoidance of the instability associated with training both together.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees and evaluates models trained on mathematical and programming problems across multiple benchmarks. Reported improvements appear for both supervised-fine-tuned models and models already trained with reinforcement learning. The findings support step-level value feedback as a useful route to improving mathematical and coding capabilities.
neurips-2025-dapo-improving-multi-step-r.tldr: DAPO improves multi-step reasoning with step-level critic feedback and independently trained actor and critic models.

paragraphs: A language model can learn what to do from examples or from a written instruction. This paper asks whether those different presentations of the same task produce a shared internal task representation. Understanding that relationship could help explain model behavior and inform methods for steering it.

The researchers study function vectors, a mechanism previously used to extract task representations from prompts containing demonstrations. They extend this approach to short textual instructions and extract instruction-based vectors that improve zero-shot task accuracy. Controls examining the contributions of each prompting form provide evidence that instruction and demonstration vectors use different model components.

The findings suggest that the two forms of prompting recruit partly overlapping mechanisms rather than a common representation through function vectors. This supplies principled support for combining instructions with demonstrations, because they can contribute through different components. It also suggests difficulties for a universal monitoring method that assumes task inference looks the same across presentation styles. The conclusion concerns the function-vector mechanism studied here.
neurips-2025-do-different-prompting-meth.tldr: Instructions and demonstrations appear to elicit different, partly overlapping task mechanisms when examined through function vectors.

paragraphs: This paper reconstructs dynamic scenes from single-camera videos containing both defocus blur and motion blur. These forms of blur arise differently, and existing approaches tend to address one at a time. Although both can be represented using blur kernels, accurately estimating those kernels is a central obstacle to handling them together.

The proposed framework predicts a blur kernel for each pixel using a network informed by scene and camera information. A blur-aware sparsity constraint helps guide those predictions. The method also dynamically adds Gaussians to address incomplete regions with too few scene elements. Information from unseen views provides an additional constraint during scene optimization.

Experiments show better photorealistic synthesis of new views than the state-of-the-art methods used for comparison. The contribution combines blur estimation with improvements to the underlying scene representation. This matters because resolving blur alone does not address incomplete reconstruction: the framework tackles both sources of difficulty when learning a dynamic scene from degraded video.
neurips-2025-dynamic-gaussian-splatting-.tldr: A unified Gaussian-splatting framework reconstructs dynamic scenes from videos containing both defocus and motion blur.

paragraphs: Continual learning must absorb new information while retaining previous knowledge. This paper argues that resisting forgetting is only part of the challenge: models also need robustness when incoming data are noisy or perturbed. DSEF addresses both goals through a Siamese backbone with static and dynamic components.

For each new task, the framework creates a lightweight expert. Its representation-optimization procedure updates the dynamic backbone while preserving representations and prediction patterns associated with earlier experts. A separate feature-fusion procedure brings robust features from historical experts into the construction of the new expert. It derives adaptive weights using mutual information to assess how relevant earlier knowledge is to the incoming task.

Together, these components aim to support rapid adaptation and useful knowledge transfer while avoiding harmful transfer. Experiments against established baselines report state-of-the-art performance, including under adversarial attacks. The stated findings support treating robustness and knowledge retention as connected design goals in online continual learning, with historical experts supplying selectively weighted information for future tasks.
neurips-2025-dynamic-siamese-expansion-f.tldr: DSEF combines expanding task experts with adaptive reuse of historical features to improve robust continual learning.

paragraphs: Removing the influence of training data becomes more complicated when a teacher model has transferred knowledge to a student. Even if the teacher can efficiently forget selected data, their influence may have spread throughout student training. Existing verified unlearning approaches can therefore leave a costly requirement to retrain the entire student.

PURGE restructures distillation so that this influence remains partitioned. It combines constituent mapping with an incremental multi-teacher strategy, restricting the impact of each teacher constituent to distinct subsets of student data. Maintaining data isolation is central to this design: it allows a teacher-side deletion to be addressed through partial student updates.

The paper supplies theoretical analysis of the resulting unlearning speed-ups and empirical evaluations across multiple datasets. These evaluations show reduced retraining overhead while keeping student accuracy comparable to standard baselines. The key contribution is making verified unlearning compatible with distillation by organizing knowledge transfer around the boundaries needed for later removal.
neurips-2025-efficient-verified-unlearni.tldr: PURGE partitions teacher-to-student knowledge transfer so verified unlearning requires only partial student retraining.

paragraphs: EraseFlow addresses removing unwanted concepts from text-to-image generators while preserving their broader generative behavior. The authors attribute difficulties in existing concept-erasure methods to an overly narrow treatment of the denoising trajectories that produce images. Their approach makes the complete generation path the object of exploration.

The framework uses a generative flow network with a trajectory-balance objective to learn a stochastic policy over denoising paths. Sampling entire trajectories lets the policy steer generation away from targeted concepts while preserving the model's prior. The method also removes the need for carefully designed reward models, which the authors connect to avoiding exploitable rewards and generalizing to unseen concepts.

Extensive empirical evaluations report better performance than existing baselines and a trade-off between erasure performance and prior preservation that the authors characterize as optimal. These findings support the paper's central idea: concept removal can benefit from shaping the sequence of denoising decisions, with attention to preserving the generator's existing capabilities throughout that process.
neurips-2025-eraseflow-learning-concept-.tldr: EraseFlow learns policies over complete denoising trajectories to erase concepts while preserving a text-to-image model's prior.

paragraphs: The extragradient method is widely used for root-finding, min-max optimization, and variational inequalities. Much of its convergence theory assumes a fixed Lipschitz bound, which restricts how quickly the problem's operator can change. This paper studies a relaxed condition that allows the bound to scale with the operator norm.

Under this alpha-symmetric (L0, L1)-Lipschitz condition, the authors introduce a new strategy for choosing extragradient step sizes. The resulting guarantees depend on the operator's structure. They establish sublinear convergence for monotone operators and linear convergence for strongly monotone operators. These are distinct rates under distinct assumptions, rather than a single guarantee for every root-finding problem.

The paper also proves local convergence for weak Minty operators, so that result applies locally rather than globally. Experiments support the theoretical analysis and demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed step sizes. The contribution extends extragradient theory to a more flexible regularity condition while retaining explicit connections between problem assumptions and convergence behavior.
neurips-2025-extragradient-method-for-l-.tldr: A new extragradient step-size strategy provides convergence guarantees under a relaxed, operator-dependent Lipschitz condition.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a transformer can learn to handle longer inputs on one task through experience with a related task. The central finding is that training on a longer auxiliary task can enable generalization to previously unseen lengths on a target task. This makes task relationships part of the explanation for length generalization.

The authors demonstrate the transfer across algorithmic problems involving arithmetic, string transformations, and maze navigation. Joint training allows models to inherit some generalization capabilities from similar tasks. Related effects also appear in pretrained language models, suggesting that pretraining can provide reusable computational structure for downstream extrapolation.

An initial mechanistic analysis finds that transfer correlates with reuse of the same attention heads across tasks. This is evidence of an association, rather than a complete causal account of transfer. Taken together, the findings support a view in which transformers can reuse learned computational structure across related tasks, helping explain some successes on inputs longer than those seen for a particular target task.
neurips-2025-extrapolation-by-associatio.tldr: Transformers can transfer length generalization from longer related tasks, with initial evidence linking transfer to shared attention heads.

paragraphs: Language-model representations mix vocabulary, syntax, meaning, and reasoning. That mixture complicates efforts to connect model features with brain activity, because strong predictions may mainly reflect simpler linguistic information. This paper develops a residual-disentanglement procedure to separate these contributions before using them to predict neural recordings.

The method first probes a language model to identify layers associated with particular features. It then successively regresses out lower-level representations, producing four nearly orthogonal embeddings corresponding to lexicon, syntax, meaning, and reasoning. The authors use these embeddings to model intracranial recordings from neurosurgical patients listening to natural speech.

The isolated reasoning embedding explains neural variation beyond the other linguistic features, including activity in visual regions outside classical language areas. Its neural signature peaks later, around 350–400 milliseconds, consistent with a processing hierarchy. The study also finds that ordinary entangled embeddings can hide these deeper contributions behind stronger shallow-feature predictions. These results support distinct reasoning-related computation during language comprehension and a more differentiated approach to comparing models with brain responses.
neurips-2025-far-from-the-shallow-brain-.tldr: Separating linguistic features from model embeddings reveals reasoning-related brain activity with distinct predictive and temporal properties.

paragraphs: HiVE-MIL tackles classification of very large pathology slides when labeled examples are scarce. Existing vision-language approaches use multiple image scales, but the authors identify weaknesses in connecting information across scales and aligning visual content with text at the same scale. Their framework models both relationships together.

It builds a unified graph with parent–child connections between coarse 5x and fine 20x visual and textual nodes. Additional edges connect visual and textual nodes within each scale. A two-stage text-guided filter removes weakly related patch–text pairs, while a hierarchical contrastive loss encourages consistent textual semantics across scales. These components combine tissue hierarchy with image–text alignment.

Experiments on TCGA breast, lung, and kidney cancer datasets show consistent improvements over traditional and recent vision-language multiple-instance learning approaches. The reported gains reach 4.1% in macro F1 in 16-shot settings. The findings support jointly modeling cross-scale structure and multimodal relationships as a useful approach to learning slide classifications from limited pathology data.
neurips-2025-few-shot-learning-from-giga.tldr: HiVE-MIL connects pathology images and text across magnifications to improve few-shot whole-slide classification.

paragraphs: Federated learning can struggle when participating clients have different data distributions. A single global model may fit those clients poorly. FLUX addresses this issue by clustering clients and using cluster-specific models, covering four common types of distribution shift during both training and testing.

The framework extracts privacy-preserving descriptors on clients and uses unsupervised clustering to organize them. It does not require advance knowledge of either the shift types or the number of clusters. It also supports adaptation for previously unseen clients without labels, allowing them to benefit from the cluster-specific models most suitable for their data.

Evaluations cover four standard benchmarks, two real-world datasets, and ten state-of-the-art baselines. The authors report improved accuracy and stability, with average accuracy gains reaching 23 percentage points over the best-performing baselines. Computational and communication overhead remain comparable to FedAvg. These results support using client descriptors to make clustered federated learning responsive to heterogeneous data and newly arriving clients.
neurips-2025-flux-efficient-descriptor-d.tldr: FLUX clusters clients using privacy-preserving descriptors and adapts cluster-specific models to unseen, unlabeled clients.

paragraphs: Edge-colored clustering organizes categorical data represented as a hypergraph, where a labeled edge can connect multiple vertices. It assigns colors to vertices while minimizing disagreements with edge colors. The paper studies extensions that allow overlapping clusters or accommodate outlier vertices, overcoming the rigid assignments of traditional edge-colored clustering.

Existing algorithms face a trade-off: linear-programming rounding produces high-quality solutions but can be expensive, while greedy combinatorial algorithms are fast but often sacrifice quality. The authors propose a family of algorithms combining linear-programming strengths with combinatorial efficiency. Their methods address Local and Global edge-colored clustering, which permit overlap, and Robust edge-colored clustering, which handles outliers.

Both theory and experiments indicate efficient production of high-quality solutions across all three problems. The paper also establishes inapproximability results and integrality-gap bounds, suggesting that substantial theoretical improvements are unlikely. These bounds help position the algorithms relative to the difficulty of the problems. The results additionally resolve two previously open questions in the literature.
neurips-2025-improved-algorithms-for-ove.tldr: New algorithms combine linear-programming quality with combinatorial efficiency for overlapping and outlier-aware hypergraph clustering.

paragraphs: Generating a video of several people speaking creates a correspondence problem: each audio stream must animate the correct person. Methods developed for a single talking face or body struggle with this assignment and can also have limited instruction-following ability. This paper introduces multi-person conversational video generation as a task and proposes MultiTalk to address it.

The authors investigate ways to inject audio into the generation process and introduce Label Rotary Position Embedding to bind audio streams to people. Training also addresses preservation of the base model's instruction-following capabilities. The authors observe that updating only part of the parameters and using multi-task training are crucial for retaining that ability.

MultiTalk achieves superior performance against compared methods on talking-head, talking-body, and multi-person datasets. The results support a framework that handles both audio–person correspondence and instruction following. Its contribution goes beyond synchronizing a single speaker by addressing the coordination required when several people and audio streams appear in one generated scene.
neurips-2025-let-them-talk-audio-driven-.tldr: MultiTalk binds separate audio streams to the correct people while preserving instruction following in conversational video generation.

paragraphs: Model Shapley measures the importance of individual language-model parameters while accounting for cooperation among them. Its starting point is that a parameter's contribution can depend on other parameters, so importance measures should capture both individual effects and synergy. The paper draws on Shapley values from cooperative game theory to express that idea.

To make parameter-level attribution scalable, the authors derive a second-order approximation using blockwise Fisher information. The approach obtains importance information through one gradient backpropagation, with mini-batch Monte Carlo updates and an efficient approximation of Hessian structure supporting the computation. The resulting scores are approximate Shapley-based attributions rather than an exhaustive accounting of every possible parameter coalition.

Experiments indicate that these attributions improve interpretability and guide more effective parameter-specific fine-tuning and compression with modest computational overhead. They also support targeted knowledge injection. The contribution is a practical way to bring cooperative parameter behavior into decisions about which parts of a large model to modify or retain.
neurips-2025-model-shapley-find-your-ide.tldr: Model Shapley approximates parameter importance while accounting for cooperation, guiding targeted fine-tuning and compression.

paragraphs: Representational Difference Explanations, or RDX, is designed to make comparisons between learned representations more understandable. The paper identifies a gap in existing post hoc explanation tools: explaining a model does not necessarily provide an effective way to contrast it with another model. RDX directly targets the differences between two representations.

The method discovers and visualizes those differences, giving comparisons an interpretable form. The authors validate it using models with known conceptual distinctions. In these tests, it recovers meaningful differences that existing explainable-AI techniques fail to reveal. Known distinctions provide a reference for assessing whether the method finds relevant contrasts.

The paper also applies RDX to state-of-the-art models on challenging subsets of ImageNet and iNaturalist. These analyses expose both differences in model representations and subtle patterns in the datasets. The stated findings support representation comparison as a useful explanatory task in its own right, helping researchers examine what separates models and what those contrasts reveal about their data.
neurips-2025-representational-difference.tldr: RDX discovers and visualizes meaningful differences between two models' learned representations.

paragraphs: Combining task-specific models can produce a single model with multiple capabilities. However, methods designed to merge fully fine-tuned models can fail when the task-specific changes are parameter-efficient modules. This paper analyzes that problem through low-rank decomposition and identifies robustness of parameter directions as a crucial factor.

The authors find that compensating for large gaps between singular values helps preserve direction robustness during merging. RobustMerge implements this idea without additional training. It prunes parameters and scales coefficients using inter-parameter relationships to stabilize directions against task interference. Cross-task normalization provides another component aimed at improving generalization to unseen tasks.

The paper introduces a benchmark spanning diverse multimodal tasks and evaluates the method's performance and generalizability on it. Additional studies support the effectiveness of the approach. The central contribution is a merging procedure tailored to the structure of parameter-efficient updates, using relationships within and across task modules to protect useful directions as their capabilities are combined.
neurips-2025-robustmerge-parameter-effic.tldr: RobustMerge combines parameter-efficient multimodal experts without training by stabilizing parameter directions and normalizing across tasks.

paragraphs: Optimal transport maps describe transformations between probability distributions. Existing estimation theory often assumes strong smoothness of the underlying Brenier potentials and bounded distribution supports. This paper develops a unified framework for semi-dual map estimation that relaxes both restrictions, expanding the settings covered by theoretical analysis.

The framework builds on a sieved convex conjugate. It establishes a map-stability bound without second-order regularity assumptions on the true potentials. An oracle inequality then separates estimation error into statistical error, sieve-induced bias, and approximation error. The approximation term uses the uniform L-infinity norm rather than a Sobolev norm, connecting the bound more naturally to classical approximation theory.

These tools yield statistical error guarantees under conditions on the true transport map that the authors describe as mild and verifiable. They also establish what they identify as the first theoretical guarantee for deep-neural-network transport-map estimation between general distributions, using Tanh networks as an example. The contribution clarifies distinct sources of error while weakening restrictive assumptions.
neurips-2025-stability-and-oracle-inequa.tldr: A new optimal-transport estimation framework weakens regularity restrictions and separates statistical, sieve, and approximation errors.

paragraphs: StruDiCO makes diffusion-based combinatorial optimization more interpretable during generation. Existing solvers can leave the solution opaque until the final step. Here, the forward process gradually deactivates variables until the solution is empty, while the reverse process selects variables incrementally, producing structurally continuous partial solutions.

A constrained consistency sampling strategy suppresses low-confidence selections to stabilize reconstruction. The framework also refines solutions during inference without computing gradients. It perturbs a current solution in a structure-aware way, reconstructs through the consistency model, and uses objective-guided scoring when decoding. This connects intermediate structure with explicit efforts to improve the optimization objective.

Experiments on the Traveling Salesman Problem and Maximal Independent Set show better solution quality than compared diffusion solvers, alongside up to 3.5 times faster inference and 70% lower GPU memory use. The reported average improvement on MIS is 38.1%. These findings support constructing meaningful partial solutions as a route to both efficient inference and useful inference-stage refinement.
neurips-2025-strudico-structured-denoisi.tldr: StruDiCO incrementally builds interpretable combinatorial solutions and refines them without gradients, improving reported efficiency and quality.

paragraphs: Data-driven optimization can work directly with observed samples or use a fitted model to choose decisions. Common approaches include sample average approximation, estimate-then-optimize, and integrated estimation-optimization. Their relative performance is difficult to characterize when the fitted model is close to correct but still imperfect.

This paper studies that intermediate case through local misspecification. Using statistical contiguity theory, the authors establish a bias–variance trade-off among the three approaches. The relative importance of bias and variance changes with the degree of local model error. This gives a more granular comparison than treating a model as simply correct or misspecified.

The analysis derives explicit expressions for decision bias and identifies directions of misspecification that do or do not affect decisions. It also provides a geometric interpretation of variance. These results explain why model error must be considered in relation to the resulting optimization decision: different departures from the assumed model can have different consequences. The framework clarifies relative performance without asserting one method is universally best.
neurips-2025-the-bias-variance-tradeoff-.tldr: Local misspecification reveals how decision bias and variance shape the relative performance of three data-driven optimization approaches.

paragraphs: TREND learns representations from LiDAR sequences without requiring labels during pretraining. Its motivation is that labeling point clouds is expensive, while successive observations naturally contain information about object motion and semantics. The method uses forecasting of future observations to turn that temporal structure into a learning signal.

A recurrent embedding scheme generates three-dimensional embeddings across time. A temporal neural field designed for LiDAR represents the scene, and differentiable rendering supplies the loss used for training. Together, these components connect the evolving representation to predicted observations, making temporal forecasting the basis of the pretraining task.

The authors evaluate the learned representations on object detection and semantic segmentation across Once, Waymo, NuScenes, and SemanticKITTI. TREND generally improves over training from scratch, with reported mAP gains of 1.77% on Once and 2.11% on NuScenes. The paper reports up to 400% more improvement than previous leading unsupervised pretraining methods. These findings support exploiting temporal LiDAR information to obtain useful representations before labeled task training.
neurips-2025-trend-unsupervised-3d-repre.tldr: TREND pretrains LiDAR representations by forecasting future observations, improving downstream detection and segmentation in reported evaluations.
